abstract: Mitochondrial matrix pH (pHmtx) regulates cellular energetics, metabolite flux, and ion transport. Despite its importance in cellular energy metabolism and disease, pHmtx remains difficult to measure in the intact heart because pH-sensitive dyes are challenging to selectively target to the mitochondrial matrix. Changes in intracellular pH during cardiac ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) are significant and understanding pHmtx dynamics I/R would provide insight into mechanisms of injury. To overcome uncertainties associated with intracellular dye distribution, the pH-sensitive green fluorescent protein SypHer3 was stably expressed in the mitochondrial matrix of the adult mouse heart using adeno-associated virus (AAV). The isolated perfused heart was subjected to global no-flow ischemia, followed by reperfusion and SypHer3 fluorescence measured using an optical integrating sphere. Calibration of SypHer3 fluorescence fold-change against pH in isolated mitochondria enabled pHmtx quantification from SypHer3 fluorescence in the intact heart, based on an assigned starting pH of 7.47. We found that pHmtx decreased from 7.45 {+/-} 0.01 (n=5) during normoxia to 6.61 {+/-} 0.20 (n=5) after 20 minutes of ischemia, and reached 7.16 {+/-} 0.01 (n=5) within 1 minute of reperfusion. In paired experiments, we measured relative changes in mitochondrial Ca2+ (Ca2+m) in the isolated heart during I/R using the genetically encoded, mitochondrial-targeted Ca2+ sensor R-GECO1. Because R-GECO1 fluorescence is pH-sensitive, quantification of pHmtx is required to correct R-GECO1 fluorescence for pH-dependent effects. With correction for pH, R-GECO1 fluorescence increased 1.77 {+/-} 0.40-fold (n=7) within 20 minutes of ischemia and returned to baseline within the first minute of reperfusion, consistent with an increase in Ca2+m during ischemia that reversed upon reperfusion. In summary, we developed a fluorescence approach for measuring pHmtx, a key determinant of mitochondrial energetics and ion transport, in the isolated perfused mouse heart, providing time resolved quantitative estimates of pHmtx during I/R. Furthermore, this work expands the application of fluorescent sensors for interrogating mitochondrial physiology in the intact heart by providing a framework for accounting for pH-dependent effects on probe fluorescence.
